title: Growth isn't required
hookLine: some people report growth after trauma and some don't, and no one owes a silver lining
last: FEAR AND BRACING ARE PART OF THE HURT.

cards: A card arrives after a hard year. On the front, in curly gold letters: everything happens for a reason. Someone meant it kindly.
Still, a line like that can land like homework. Find the reason. Write up the lesson.
Show your growth by Friday. Two psychologists studied what happens to people after terrible events, and what they found is more honest than the card. Some people do grow.
Some don't. And the card leaves out the most important part: growth isn't required.

teach.b: First, the name. Richard Tedeschi and Lawrence Calhoun, psychologists who studied people after trauma, gave one pattern a name: posttraumatic growth.
Some of the people they studied described changes on the far side of the struggle. Closer relationships. New priorities.
A sense of their own strength. A deeper spiritual life. Second, the fine print.

teach.h: IT COMES FROM THE STRUGGLE, NOT THE EVENT.
teach.b: In their account, the growth comes out of the struggle with what happened, not out of the event itself. The disaster isn't the teacher.
And growth and distress can sit side by side: a person can report real growth and still hurt.
Third, not everyone reports it. Their work describes growth as something some people find, not a stage everyone reaches, and not a test anyone passes or fails. Nobody owes the world a silver lining.
Fourth, an old text that makes room for this.
Earlier this year, this path read Psalm thirteen, a complaint that turns toward trust by its last verse. Psalm eighty-eight doesn't turn.

It's a prayer from the bottom, and its last line in the King James Bible is this: "Lover and friend hast thou put far from me, and mine acquaintance into darkness." That's where it stops. No lesson, no bright side.
And it sits in the Bible of Jews and Christians alike, ending and all. Some readers take comfort in exactly that: a holy book that lets a sufferer end in the dark without being told to cheer up.
Growth may come, quietly, later on. Or it may not. Either way, the hard thing doesn't have to earn its keep.

how: Psychologists who study posttraumatic growth describe it as something some people report after a struggle, not a requirement; Jews and Christians keep Psalm 88, a prayer that ends in darkness, in their scriptures.

o: the idea that every trauma makes a person stronger
growth some people report after struggling with trauma
the body slowly healing after a serious injury

games.q: after hard things — tap the pairs.
p: Tedeschi and Calhoun's name for it

s: the researchers say everyone who goes through trauma grows from it

in their account, the growth comes from the terrible event itself

games.q: a friend's terrible year is finally over. you're writing in their card. what do you write?
o: here's what this year taught you.
that sounded so hard. I'm here.
at least it made you stronger.
games.why: today's lesson: some people report growth after a struggle and some don't, and no one owes a silver lining. even Psalm 88 is allowed to end in the dark.

practice: Bring to mind one hard thing, past or present, not the hardest. If the mind rushes to ask what it taught you, let that question sit down: it happened, it hurt, and that's enough to say.
If you pray, you can offer it with no moral attached; if a lesson shows up on its own, let it come, just don't go digging for one.

wordCard.voice: Posttraumatic growth, the pattern Tedeschi and Calhoun named in some survivors of trauma: closer relationships, new priorities, a sense of their own strength. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: that sounds hard. Sometimes those three words are the whole kindness. Go gently.

sources.work: Richard G. Tedeschi and Lawrence G. Calhoun, research on posttraumatic growth
